biography.value: A greying man of about fifty in the mud-stiff grey-and-oak cassock of a Ridgeward battalion chaplain, walking backwards ahead of his column so he can keep an eye on them, cheerfully counting heads that are not there.

description.value:
He walks the line with a hand out, touching shoulders that are mostly not there, saying something over each of them too quietly to catch.

Action, 1/day. Ambrose casts Bless on up to three of his men within 30 ft. For 1 minute (concentration — and he is a terrible concentrator; [ASK PLAYER] any damage he takes, DC 10 or the higher of 10 / half the damage, and he loses it), each blessed skeleton adds 1d4 to every attack roll and every saving throw.

At +4 to hit, a blessed skeleton is swinging at roughly +6.5. That is real, it is one action he is not spending on On Your Feet, and it ends the moment somebody makes him lose concentration — which is one more reason to go through him instead of around him.

He is not buffing troops. He thinks he is saying a blessing over tired men before a hard stretch of road, and he is right about the second half of that.

Prerequisite: Once per day. He usually spends it in round 2, the round after the first man goes down — or before a river crossing, or a hill, or anything he has decided is difficult for them.

activation.condition: Once per day. He usually spends it in **round 2**, the round after the first man goes down — or before a river crossing, or a hill, or anything he has decided is difficult for them.

description.value:
"...Halt." Very quietly. And then, in the parade-ground voice, and it cracks: "COLUMN. HALT."

THE CONTROLLER-BREAK. This is the mechanic the variant exists for — state it to the table as a rule, not a ruling.

The skeletons here are not independently animate. They are following him. The instant the prerequisite above is met, then at the start of the next skeleton's turn, every remaining skeleton stops where it stands, mid-swing. Immediate, automatic, no roll. They stand still for one full round.

Then, at the end of that round: - He is still down or still stopped → every skeleton turns west and reverts to Shamble Onward. v1 rules resume exactly: no attacks unless individually damaged, blocked, or grabbed; no pursuit. The fight is over unless the party restarts it. - He got free → he can start them again, but it costs his entire action (the_column_moves). Every time.

Make it findable. He announces On Your Feet out loud, by name, every single time he uses it. He is telling the party how to beat him and he does not know that is what he is doing. A party that stands in the open trading swings loses slowly; a party that grabs the chaplain wins in two rounds. That is the lesson.

description.value:
He says the man's name. Then he says who is waiting for him, and where, and how far.

Reaction, no roll, no mechanical effect — this is a voice tool and it is the best thing he does. The first time one of his men goes down within 30 ft, Ambrose names him aloud: rank, company, home village, and the person expecting him. He is not accusing anybody. He is doing the only part of his job he has left.

It is also the switch. From his NEXT turn onward the party are deserters and grave-robbers, and radiant_flame comes off the shelf. Until this fires, he does not attack at all.

If it is the skeleton wearing the corroded bronze pauldron — Corwin Caldor — use this, verbatim, and let it land:

> "Corwin Caldor. Third company, Ridgeward. He has a wife at Ardenford — Maris. He talks about her. He talks about her the entire time, he does not stop." (He is smiling.) "I promised him I'd get him to the door."

The party were sent here by that man's grandson. Do not explain that to the table. They will get there.

Once per round; refreshes at the start of his turn. If you need more names for the other men, take them off the third company muster roll in his satchel: Serjeant Callow, Ostry, Penn, the Byrne boy who was seventeen.

description.value:
For one second he is not confused at all. "Oh. — I did lose them, didn't I."

The non-violent solve. It is the good ending and it pays FULL encounter XP — say so out loud.

This is not necromancy and never was. It is a burial rite, interrupted a hundred and twenty-seven years ago by the Calderon second wave, still running because nobody ever said the last third of the words. Ambrose is the officiant. The reason nothing on this field can rest is that by the time it was his turn, there was nobody left standing to say them over him.

[ASK PLAYER] DC 15 Religion or History, one action, spoken aloud.

Success: the procession ends. Every skeleton lies down where it stands, without drama, the way a man sits down after a long day. Ambrose says his last line — "See them the rest of the way." — and is not there any more. A cassock, a mace, and the third company muster roll on the stones.

Failure: nothing bad happens. He doesn't notice, doesn't take offence, doesn't retaliate, doesn't get a free attack. Try again next round, as many times as they like.

There is NO Persuasion answer. No DC makes him understand what he is. A natural 20 on Persuasion buys a kind, attentive, completely useless reply. The delusion holds because he could not survive it breaking, and something in him knows that.

description.value:
He walks backwards ahead of them so he can keep an eye on the column, counting heads that are not there, apologising for the delay.

Default action, every round, until the party makes this a fight. Ambrose moves west with his men at the column's pace, calls the cadence, checks on them by name, and tries to give the party jobs — water, a hand with the cart, directions to the ford. He makes no attack and orders no attack. While he is doing this, the skeletons run v1 rules exactly: Shamble Onward, no hostility, no pursuit, provoked only individually. The party has the whole scene to decide what this is.

He never opens the fight. Not if they draw, not if they block the road, not if they insult him. The first violence on this field is always the party's.

This action is also how he restarts a broken column. If the procession was broken (he was at 0 HP, grappled, restrained, incapacitated, held prone, or unable to speak) and he has since gotten free, restarting the march costs his entire action — no attack, no raise, nothing else, that turn. Grappling him twice is a legitimate strategy and it should cost him two full turns.

Voice: warm, brisk, unhurried, busy. He interrupts himself to check the column. He calls everyone "gentlemen" and doesn't notice. He is never cruel and never wrong about anything except the one fact at the centre of him: the battle was three days ago, and the men are tired, not dead.

biography.value: A yellowed human skeleton in the rotted grey-and-oak livery of the Ridgeward Battalion, walking west with unhurried, purposeful steps, empty sockets fixed on something a hundred and twenty-seven years gone.

description.value:
The skull turns toward the voice and stops. Whatever is left in there is listening.

The skeleton halts and orients on the speaker. [ASK PLAYER] DC 13 Persuasion or Religion check. Success: the skeletons are not hostile — they are confused, and they are going home. They stand still while a calm voice keeps talking, and can be led, turned, or walked elsewhere. Failure: no harm done and no aggression triggered; the skeleton resumes Shamble Onward on its next turn and the party may try again. It understands the languages it knew in life but cannot speak and will not answer questions — it responds to tone, not words.

Prerequisite: A PC addresses the skeleton calmly instead of attacking it, and no attack has been made against it this round.

activation.condition: A PC addresses the skeleton calmly instead of attacking it, and no attack has been made against it this round.

description.value:
It walks. Empty sockets fixed west, it steps around the living the way a man steps around a fencepost.

Default action, every round, unless this skeleton has been damaged, blocked, or grabbed. The skeleton moves its full 30 ft. west toward Ardenford and makes no attack. It steps around a creature standing in its path — once. If a PC blocks it a second time, grabs it, or damages it, it counts as threatened and switches to Shortsword or Shortbow from its next turn on. A skeleton that is disengaged from does not pursue: it reorients west and resumes walking. No morale, no fear, no retreat — once provoked it fights to 0 HP, and walks the rest of the time.

description.value:
It comes free with a wet sound, hangs heavy in the air for a beat, and climbs out of reach.

The stirge spends 5 ft of its movement to detach, then flies with the rest of its 40 ft straight up and out of melee reach — moving away from an attached host this way does not provoke, but leaving a threatened space does, so use the ceiling. A gorged stirge (two drains) leaves the encounter entirely: it goes back to the roof-dark to digest and does not come down again. A damaged stirge circles at 20+ ft for a round, then picks a different target. Stirges have no loyalty to each other and no morale to break — they are not a faction, they are weather. Killing them all is optional; the party can simply leave.

Prerequisite: Either the stirge has drained twice (it is gorged and done), or it has taken any damage at all while attached — at 5 HP a stirge does not survive a second hit and it has no interest in finding out.

activation.condition: Either the stirge has drained **twice** (it is gorged and done), **or** it has taken any damage at all while attached -- at 5 HP a stirge does not survive a second hit and it has no interest in finding out.

description.value:
The sound registers first and nobody can place it: a dry leathery flutter, directly overhead, getting closer.

The stirges detach from the ceiling and drop. Roll initiative for them now and slot them into the existing order. Each picks the nearest warm body and goes for exposed skin — neck, forearm, scalp. They have no interest in the fight anyone else is having and they do not care whose side anyone is on: a stirge will land on a smuggler as happily as on a paladin. Flying 40 ft with only 10 ft on the ground: they stay off the floor, they cannot be flanked, and a PC who wants to hit one in the air had better have reach or a bow.

Prerequisite: Do not roll these into initiative at the top of the fight. They come down mid-fight — DM's call, but the good beat is the start of round 2 or 3, or the moment somebody shouts, or the first time a torch goes up. They were always there.

Note: Compare to each PC's passive Perception. Beat it and the stirge's first Proboscis attack is made with advantage against a surprised target. This is one roll for the whole flight — do not roll it per stirge.

description.value:
It puts a flat hand out sideways — not at the party, at its own people. "That's it. That's enough."

The tough stops fighting and starts talking, and its side stops with it. It is not begging: it names terms and it means them. Terms are always some version of you get what you came for, we walk away breathing, nobody says a name to anybody. If the party keeps swinging after this, the tough fights to 0 HP and so does everyone still standing — the offer does not come twice. [ASK PLAYER] DC 12 Persuasion or Intimidation to close on the offered terms, or better; on a hard failure the tough takes the deal off the table and goes back to work. If the party accepts, the encounter is over — award full XP.

Prerequisite: Fires the moment the tough thinks the price has gone past the point of the job: it is at or below half HP, or two of its side are down, or a PC makes it a credible offer. The tough is the only one here who can end this for everybody, and it knows it.

biography.value: A grey, water-swollen thing in the rotted red of a Calderon field coat, moving at a steady walking pace with its head slightly turned, as if listening to something behind it.

description.value:
The head turns toward the voice. Something behind the face registers that a sound happened, and then it takes another step.

There is nothing in here to talk to. Heed the Living does not work on the zombie — no check, no DC, no partial success. Where a skeleton stops and listens to tone, this one has kept enough meat to rot and lost whatever the skeletons kept. It closes at its full 20 ft and slams the nearest living thing. This is the point of the variant: a party that solves the battlefield with a gentle voice gets three skeletons standing quiet in a ring and one dead Calderon soldier still walking through the middle of them, and now they have to decide what to do about him while the others watch. No morale, no fear, no retreat, no pursuit beyond what it can reach at 20 ft.

Prerequisite: A PC tries a calm voice on it — or the skeletons have already been talked down and someone assumes this one will follow.

activation.condition: A PC tries a calm voice on it -- or the skeletons have already been talked down and someone assumes this one will follow.
